summary: A 1977 description of the NAME/FINGER protocol, which lets a user ask a remote host who is logged in or for information about a user. It was later replaced by RFC 1194, RFC 1196 and RFC 1288.

plainLanguage.summary: This 1977 note describes a simple way to ask a distant computer who is using it right now, or for a short report about one person. You connect, send a single line of text, and read back a friendly answer. It became known as Finger.

subtitle: A 1977 note describing how to ask a remote host who is logged in, or about one user, with a single line.

tldr.problem: Sites had programs giving friendly status reports on who was on the system or about a person, but no way to ask them across the network.
tldr.mechanism: The client connects to socket 117 octal, 79 decimal, sends one command line ending in CRLF, and reads the report until the server closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: Later specifications RFC 1194, RFC 1196 and RFC 1288 replaced it.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 742 as Unknown and obsoleted by RFC 1194, RFC 1196 and RFC 1288. It is the early description of the Finger protocol.

sections.title: What NAME/FINGER Is
sections.content:
The Name/Finger protocol provides an interface to the Name and Finger programs at several network sites. These programs return a friendly, human-oriented status report on either the system at the moment or one particular person in depth.

When the RFC was written, only the SAIL, SRI and ITS sites supported it, though other systems with similar programs could easily become servers. There is no required report format; the protocol consists mostly of specifying a single command line.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like asking the front desk who is here right now, or whether a particular person is in, and getting a friendly answer.

sections.title: Using the Protocol
sections.content:
The client does an ICP to socket 117 octal (79 decimal) and establishes two 8-bit connections, sends a single command line ending in CRLF, and receives information that varies with the line and the system. The server closes its connections as soon as the output is finished.

A null line, that is just a CRLF, asks the server for a default report listing all people using the system at that moment. A user name such as FOO asks about only that user, whether logged in or not. ITS and SAIL sites allow several comma-separated names, and an ITS server returns fuller descriptions if the /W switch appears on the line.
sections.plainLanguage: You send one line. A blank line means who is here, and a name means tell me about this person.

sections.title: What the Reports Contain
sections.content:
The default listing should include at least each user's full name and the physical location of their terminal where it can be determined. Job name and idle time are also reasonable and useful.

For a named user who is logged in, a line or two in the same format is returned, showing only that user. If the user is not logged in, the expected reply gives the full name and the time of last logout. There is also a plan feature, a short message the user leaves that is included in such responses, easily implemented by reading a specially named text file. If a name is ambiguous, all possible matches should be returned; SAIL lists the possible names and no more, while an ITS server gives the full standard information for each.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a short card about each person: their name, where their terminal is and how long they have been quiet. People can also leave a note that gets shown to anyone who asks about them.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
Anyone wishing to implement such a server is encouraged to contact the maintainers of NAME at MIT-AI, where a list of all sites with such servers is kept. The RFC also suggests extending local programs so they can name other sites, for example :NAME @SAIL on ITS to get SAIL's default listing.

Connecting directly to the server from a TIP or a simple Telnet user program can send option negotiations that foul up the command line interpretation, so a server may filter out IAC bytes and respond negatively, IAC WON'T, to option commands. This is a convenience, not a requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Some dial-in programs send extra chatter that can confuse the answering computer, so the server is allowed to ignore the chatter and say no to it.
